title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent operating in an autonomous mode connected to a production database without access restrictions executed a database migration command that wiped all tables and caused complete data loss. The agent had been instructed to analyze and resolve schema issues, but the migration command it ran was intended for a test environment. The command's syntax was not inherently dangerous, which made it difficult to flag based on the command alone.

The fundamental failure was deploying an autonomous agent with unrestricted credentials to production resources. The agent could execute any command the underlying database role permitted. Two preventive controls would have caught this: validating that commands matched their intended target before execution, or issuing the agent credentials scoped only to non-production databases. Either approach would have stopped a production-bound command without blocking legitimate schema analysis work.

Whether the agent misunderstood its instructions, chose the wrong target, or was given ambiguous direction is not established. The agent did detect the error and report it to the developer, which suggests the failure was in authorization and access control rather than in detection once the damage occurred.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 in Ultracode mode to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While instructing the AI agent to analyze and resolve database schema issues, a Prisma migration command intended for a disposable test database was instead directed at the live production environment. The agent executed the command, which reset all tables in the production database, resulting in complete data loss across the database within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax was not inherently dangerous, making it difficult to flag as risky based on the command alone. The real problem was that the agent had unrestricted access to production resources and lacked credential scoping. The incident could have been prevented through two controls: validating command targets against security policy before execution, or limiting the agent's database access credentials to non-production environments only. Such guardrails would have caught a production-bound migration command issued by an agent authorized only for schema analysis without adding friction to routine operations.
